1. Video: Steering Long Sessions
You can prompt Claude and watch it finish a quick task, but running a long one is much harder. Refactoring across a dozen files or implementing a new feature can take hours, and if you aren't steering Claude in the right direction, it can potentially take longer. But there are many ways to help Claude during these long sessions. There are two important habits. The first is to scope the work before Claude starts. So if you use plan mode, Claude will do the research in read-only mode and hand you a plan. If the plan has been provided, actually read through it. The more thorough the plan, the less likely that you're going to have hiccups when Claude executes. And when it comes to revising the plan, just ask Claude to add it where you want. It's much faster to iterate over a plan than it is to simply hope for the best. The second habit is to steer Claude in the right direction. And here are some ways that you can do that. Compact summarizes your conversation and uses that as a new context while deleting the old, freeing up your context window. However, there is a risk that something important will be removed, causing Claude to drift in the wrong direction. So when you do the compact command, add in the changes you want. And adding instructions after the command tells Claude how to summarize. So if you were done debugging a while ago but want to just focus on those API changes, well here you can do that. When Claude goes down the wrong path, you don't have to prompt your way out of it. Rewind brings you to the last checkpoint. To open it, double tap escape on an empty prompt and you'll get the rewind menu. Every user prompt creates a checkpoint that you can revert back to with different options. One, you can restore the code, conversation, or both. Two, summarize from here will summarize everything after the checkpoint. Great if you had a side conversation and just want to free up some space. And summarize up to here will summarize everything before the checkpoint. So this is great if you want to summarize a long setup phase, but keep the implementation parts. When we talk about steering, we assume that you are hands-on. If you want something a little bit more autonomous, there is the goal and loop. Goal sets a completion condition. You describe what done looks like and Claude keeps working across turns until a fast evaluator confirms that those conditions have been met. Instead of just stopping for the first time, it thinks it's finished. So for example, I could do /goal, all tests in source billing, pass, and the type checker report zero errors. Doing /goal clear will cancel it. And one constraint here is that the evaluator only reads the transcript, so the condition has to be checkable from the output that Claude produces, like the test results that it ran. Loop runs a prompt on an interval between turns, fixed or self-paced. Use it to pull something external like a CI run or a deploy and act when the state changes. You can press escape to stop it. So our steering metaphor assumes one steering wheel in one car. But when we're working with multiple agents on the same code base, we don't want to have two steering wheels in one car. Well, that's just unsafe. This is where work trees come in. It prevents two or more Claude sessions from fighting over files in a repository. This prevents conflicts by having three independent file trees. On exit, a clean work tree is auto removed. A dot work tree include file at the repo root lists gitignored files to copy into each work tree, which is useful for a environment variable file or a local configuration that you need, but don't want to commit into the version control. When it comes to handling long Claude Code sessions, scope your work first and then steer. Direct your compaction so the summary keeps what matters. Use the rewind menu to course correct. Set a goal when you can describe done better than you can describe the steps and run parallel work and work trees. Do that and you can trust a long run without babysitting it.

question.en:
Read the article, then answer the question below.

For the rest of this course you'll be working on queries, a small project your team uses to pull reports out of an online store's database: which orders are still pending, what stock is running low, who your best customers are.

Right now you are three hours into a Claude Code session on it. The first hour went on a database connection bug, which you fixed and moved past. Since then you have been building an alert for orders left pending too long, and the context window is filling up. Your next task builds directly on that alert.

Which move frees up the context window while keeping the work that matters?
question.fr:
Lisez l'article, puis répondez à la question ci-dessous.

Pour le reste de ce cours, vous travaillerez sur queries, un petit projet que votre équipe utilise pour extraire des rapports de la base de données d'une boutique en ligne : quelles commandes sont encore en attente, quel stock commence à manquer, qui sont vos meilleurs clients.

Vous êtes actuellement à trois heures d'une Claude Code session dessus. La première heure a été consacrée à un bug de connexion à la base de données, que vous avez corrigé. Depuis, vous construisez une alerte pour les commandes restées en attente trop longtemps, et la fenêtre de contexte se remplit. Votre prochaine tâche s'appuie directement sur cette alerte.

Quelle action libère la fenêtre de contexte tout en conservant le travail important ?

text.en: Run /compact on its own and let Claude decide what the summary keeps.
text.fr: Exécutez /compact seul et laissez Claude décider ce que le résumé conserve.

text.en: Double tap escape and restore the code and conversation to the last checkpoint.
text.fr: Appuyez deux fois sur escape et restaurez le code et la conversation au dernier checkpoint.

text.en: Run /compact Focus on the pending-orders alert implementation, so the summary keeps that thread.
text.fr: Exécutez /compact Focus on the pending-orders alert implementation, afin que le résumé conserve ce fil.

text.en: Run /clear and re-explain the task from scratch.
text.fr: Exécutez /clear et réexpliquez la tâche depuis le début.

explanation.en: Great choice! Anything you type after /compact shapes the summary. Naming the thread you are still working on carries it through compaction while the finished debugging detour falls away.
explanation.fr: Excellent choix ! Tout ce que vous tapez après /compact façonne le résumé. Nommer le fil sur lequel vous travaillez encore le fait passer à travers la compaction, tandis que la parenthèse de débogage terminée s'efface.

hint.en:
Anything you type after /compact tells Claude how to summarize, so the summary keeps the thread you name.

Rewind and /clear both throw work away, while compaction is the move that frees space and carries the session forward.
hint.fr:
Tout ce que vous tapez après /compact indique à Claude comment résumer, donc le résumé conserve le fil que vous nommez.

Rewind et /clear suppriment tous deux du travail, tandis que la compaction est l'action qui libère de l'espace et permet à la session d'avancer.

Enter plan mode with /plan, then ask Claude to plan the work described in task.md. If there are initial follow-up questions from Claude, answer them any way you wish.

blocks.starterCode:
repl = connect('bash')
# Strip the redundant Write() allow rule the image seeds into
# ~/.claude/settings.json. Newer Claude Code versions warn about it on every
# launch, since file permission checks only match Edit() rules and
# Edit(/home/repl/**) already covers every file-editing tool.
repl.run_command('''python3 - <<'PY'
import json
p = '/home/repl/.claude/settings.json'
try:
    settings = json.load(open(p))
    perms = settings.get('permissions', {})
    perms['allow'] = [r for r in perms.get('allow', []) if not r.startswith('Write(')]
    json.dump(settings, open(p, 'w'), indent=2)
except Exception:
    pass
PY''')
# The shipped hooks launch a nested Claude session on every edit, which would
# slow this exercise down. Chapter 2 wires hooks up deliberately instead.
repl.run_command('rm -f /home/repl/queries/.claude/settings.local.json')
repl.run_command('cd /home/repl/queries && rm -f ~/.claude/history.jsonl'
                 # Transcripts outlive history.jsonl, so a previous exercise's
                 # answers would otherwise be graded as this one's.
                 ' && rm -rf ~/.claude/projects/-home-repl-queries && clear')

hint.en:
The rewind menu works backwards over what already happened, restoring code or conversation to a checkpoint, or summarizing either side of it.

A goal sets a completion condition, and Claude keeps working across turns until a fast evaluator confirms the condition is met.

Worktrees give each session its own independent file tree, so parallel agents cannot clobber each other's changes.
hint.fr:
Le rewind menu parcourt en sens inverse ce qui s'est déjà passé, restaurant le code ou la conversation à un point de contrôle, ou en résumant l'une ou l'autre de ses parties.

Un goal définit une condition d'achèvement, et Claude continue de travailler à travers les tours jusqu'à ce qu'un évaluateur rapide confirme que la condition est remplie.

Les Worktrees donnent à chaque session son propre arbre de fichiers indépendant, afin que des agents parallèles ne puissent pas écraser les modifications des autres.

blocks.transcript:
1. Video: A CLAUDE.md That Follows
The CLAUDE.md file is not an enforced configuration, meaning if you keep adding to one gigantic file, the less Claude is able to follow it correctly. Here's how you can keep your CLAUDE.md file tight and to follow your instructions much more reliably. Simply put, the longer the file gets, the more it has to compete with itself. First, is CLAUDE.md even the right tool for the job? A hard rule like never push to main belongs in a PreToolUse hook instead. The hook is designed to stop the push even when Claude does try to do it. The CLAUDE.md file doesn't just exist in your project file, there's three other places. One's your managed policy, then your user file, then your project file, and finally local. Claude loads every memory file together. Nothing gets dropped, and org-policy is always in play. Local is for what's just yours in this project. Say you're refactoring off the sprint and want Claude to hold your architectural decisions in mind. That goes in local, not the shared project file. To make your CLAUDE.md files easier to maintain, use the path-to-file syntax to split up your instructions. Just know what they buy you, though. Claude expands imported files inline at launch right alongside the file that references them. Imports help you organize a large CLAUDE.md file, but everything still loads up front and they don't reduce context. So we can make our CLAUDE.md file much shorter. Whether Claude obeys it comes down to phrasing, and most rules fail because they're pretty vague. First, be specific and checkable. Don't put things like, follow best practices. Do you even know what that means? Well, don't expect Claude to magically. Put new API routes in source API handlers, one per file. Well, that's explicit, so put that instead. Name the replacement. Don't use default exports. Leave the alternative open. Use name exports, not default exports. Close that potential misinterpretation. And then realize that emphasis is a budget. Important and you must raises a rule priority, but only relative to everything quieter around it. Spend them on the two or three rules that hurt when broken. The file also stays under revision. When Claude does the wrong thing, well, treat that as a bug report against your CLAUDE.md file. Tell it, add that to the CLAUDE.md file, and it'll write that rule for you. Treat your CLAUDE.md file like production code. If you can't justify a line, well, delete it. Move enforcement to hooks, organize with imports, and scope past specific conventions into your rules so that they load only when they apply. The leaner the file, the more of it Claude follows.

question.en:
Read the article, then answer the question below.

The CLAUDE.md in your queries project has grown to 200 lines. You just tidied it by splitting the rules into three files and importing them with the path-to-file syntax. The file reads beautifully now. Claude still skips the same rules it skipped before.

What actually changed, and what should you do next?
question.fr:
Lisez l'article, puis répondez à la question ci‑dessous.

Le CLAUDE.md de votre projet queries a atteint 200 lignes. Vous venez de le ranger en scindant les règles en trois fichiers et en les important avec la syntaxe path-to-file. Le fichier est maintenant très lisible. Claude ignore encore les mêmes règles qu'il ignorait auparavant.

Qu'est‑ce qui a réellement changé, et que devriez‑vous faire ensuite ?

text.en: Imported files load only when Claude needs them, so move the remaining rules into imports as well.
text.fr: Les fichiers importés ne sont chargés que lorsque Claude en a besoin, donc déplacez aussi les règles restantes dans des imports.

text.en: The four memory locations are conflicting, so delete the user-level file and let the project file win.
text.fr: Les quatre emplacements de Memory sont en conflit : supprimez le fichier au niveau utilisateur et laissez le fichier du projet l'emporter.

text.en: Add IMPORTANT to every rule so that Claude stops skipping them.
text.fr: Ajoutez IMPORTANT à chaque règle afin que Claude cesse de les ignorer.

text.en: Nothing about the context load changed, because imports expand inline at launch. Delete the rules you cannot justify and make the ones that remain specific and checkable.
text.fr: Rien dans le chargement du contexte n’a changé, car les imports sont développés en ligne au lancement. Supprimez les règles que vous ne pouvez pas justifier et faites en sorte que celles qui restent soient spécifiques et vérifiables.

explanation.en: Spot on. Imports are an organizing tool, not a way to shrink what Claude reads. The file competes with itself until you cut it down, so the fix is fewer rules, each one specific enough that you could check whether it was followed.
explanation.fr: Bien vu. Les imports sont un outil d'organisation, pas un moyen de réduire ce que Claude lit. Le fichier se fait concurrence à lui‑même tant que vous ne le réduisez pas, donc la solution est d'avoir moins de règles, chacune suffisamment spécifique pour que vous puissiez vérifier si elle a été respectée.

hint.en:
Imports organize a long file, but Claude expands them inline at launch, so the same amount of text still loads.

All four memory locations load together and stack, and emphasis only raises a rule relative to the quieter rules around it.

question.en:
Read the article, then answer the question below.

You packaged your team's post-refactor checks into a skill at .claude/skills/verify-changes/. Its frontmatter is two lines: the name is verify-changes, and the description reads, in full, Verification skill.

The steps in the body are solid, and whenever you ask for the skill by name it runs perfectly. What it never does is fire on its own. Every time Claude finishes a refactor you end up asking for the check by name, which is the exact habit the skill was meant to replace.

Why isn't the skill firing by itself?
question.fr:
Lisez l'article, puis répondez à la question ci‑dessous.

Vous avez empaqueté les vérifications post-refactor de votre équipe dans une skill à .claude/skills/verify-changes/. Son frontmatter fait deux lignes : le name est verify-changes, et la description se lit, en entier, "Verification skill".

Les étapes dans le corps sont solides, et chaque fois que vous demandez la skill par son nom elle s'exécute parfaitement. Ce qu'elle ne fait jamais, c'est se déclencher toute seule. À chaque fois que Claude termine un refactor, vous vous retrouvez à demander la vérification par son nom, ce qui est exactement l'habitude que la skill était censée remplacer.

Pourquoi la skill ne se déclenche-t-elle pas d'elle-même ?

text.en: Skills only ever run when you invoke them by name, so firing on their own is not something they do.
text.fr: Les skills ne s'exécutent que lorsque vous les invoquez par leur nom, donc le fait de se déclencher tout seul n'en fait pas partie.

text.en: The description is what triggers a skill, and "Verification skill" describes nothing, so it never matches the task Claude just finished.
text.fr: C'est la description qui déclenche une skill, et "Verification skill" ne décrit rien, donc elle ne correspond jamais à la tâche que Claude vient d'achever.

text.en: The procedure in SKILL.md is too long, and Claude skips skills over a certain size.
text.fr: La procédure dans SKILL.md est trop longue, et Claude ignore les skills au-delà d'une certaine taille.

text.en: Verification is a standing convention, so the steps belong in CLAUDE.md instead.
text.fr: La vérification est une convention permanente, donc les étapes appartiennent plutôt à CLAUDE.md.

explanation.en: That's it exactly. The description is the trigger. Something like "Run after refactors or edits to source files: runs the test suite, reads the diff, and confirms no test was weakened" gives Claude something to match against, so the skill fires without you asking.

hint.en:
Only skill descriptions load into context until a skill is actually needed, so the description is what has to carry the trigger.

A skill folder can also hold reference files and scripts, which Claude reaches for only once the skill is running.

Read the article, then answer the question below.

You left Claude refactoring the queries project's authentication module overnight in auto mode, working on a branch on your own machine. Nothing was pushed and nothing was deployed. The classifier stopped nothing, the run finished clean, and the summary reads well: every caller migrated, every check green.

This morning you pull the branch up, start the app, and nobody can log in.

Why didn't auto mode catch this, and what should you add?
question.fr:
Lisez l'article, puis répondez à la question ci‑dessous.

Vous avez laissé Claude refactorer le module d'authentification du projet queries pendant la nuit en auto mode, en travaillant sur une branche sur votre machine locale. Rien n'a été poussé et rien n'a été déployé. Le classifier n'a rien arrêté, le run s'est terminé proprement, et le résumé est bon : chaque appelant a été migré, toutes les vérifications sont au vert.

Ce matin, vous récupérez la branche, lancez l'application, et personne ne peut se connecter.

Pourquoi l'auto mode n'a-t-il pas détecté cela, et que devriez-vous ajouter ?

text.en: Auto mode only reviews file edits, so the bash commands in the run slipped past unreviewed.
text.fr: Auto mode ne passe en revue que les modifications de fichiers, donc les commandes bash de l'exécution sont passées sans être examinées.

text.en: The classifier failed open because the run was unattended, since it only reviews actions while someone is watching.
text.fr: Le classifier a «failed open» parce que l'exécution était sans surveillance : il ne passe en revue les actions que lorsqu'une personne regarde.

text.en: The classifier reviews intent, not correctness. Broken code isn't dangerous, so it was waved through. Pair auto mode with a stop hook that runs your checks.

text.fr: Vous voulez que Claude travaille sans vous solliciter, mais que chaque action soit vérifiée pour les risques avant d'être exécutée.

text.en: A CI pipeline that should deny anything outside its pre-approved tool list rather than stall on a prompt.
text.fr: Un pipeline CI qui doit refuser tout ce qui ne figure pas sur sa liste d'outils préapprouvés plutôt que de rester bloqué en attendant une invite.

text.en: A scheduled overnight job with no human present, where unapproved actions should be refused silently.
text.fr: Un travail planifié de nuit sans intervention humaine, où les actions non approuvées doivent être refusées silencieusement.

Don't ask maintient les pipelines non supervisés en marche en refusant tout ce qui n'est pas sur la liste approuvée. Bypass permissions n'a sa place que dans des conteneurs et VM isolés.

Auto is the hands-off default: Claude runs without prompting while a classifier reviews each action for danger before it executes.

Don't ask allows only pre-approved tools and auto-denies everything else with no prompt, which is what keeps an unattended pipeline moving.

Bypass permissions skips every check, so it is only safe where there is nothing outside the sandbox left to damage.

1. Video: Hooks
A hook is a deterministic code at a fixed point in the loop, which means it can guarantee far more than formatting on a run you're not watching. It turns a rule from "Claude usually listens" into "Claude can't skip it". Claude Code fires around 30 hook events. The handful you'll reach for is PreToolUse, which fires before a tool call, the enforcement primitive, PostToolUse, which fires after a successful tool call. This is usually where auto-formatting or an auto-lint would go. Stop, which fires when Claude wants to end its turn. Refuse, if conditions aren't met. SubAgentStop is the same signal, but for subagent finishing. Precompact and Postcompact fire before and after compaction. To re-inject context after compaction, use SessionStart with the compact matcher, not postcompact. InstructionsLoaded fires when a CLAUDE.md or rule file loads. Audit what made it into context. SessionStart primes the environment. Check SourceStartup to run only on fresh starts. For PreToolUse, return JSON and exit 0 with a permission, decision field, allow, deny, or ask. There's a fourth value, defer, but it only applies to non-interactive, dash p runs, where a calling process pauses the tool and resumes it later, so you'll rarely reach for it. You can also return updatedInput to modify the tool call without blocking, which can be useful for redacting secrets out of a bash command. One catch is that updatedInput replaces the whole input object, so echo back the fields that you aren't changing. For hooks that don't return JSON, exit codes work too. So, here's the three numbers that matter. 0 is a success, so if the standard out is JSON, Claude parses it. Plain text is ignored on most events, but on SessionStart, userPromPsubmit, and userPromPromPexp, it gets added to context, which is exactly what makes the state preserver work. 2 is a blocking error, so standard error gets fed back to Claude as a context. This is the blocking exit code almost everywhere, where the lone exception, worktree create, aborts any non-zero code. Watch out, because exit1 feels like an error, but it actually does not block, so Claude runs the command anyway. And then anything else is non-blocking and is locked. Exit2 can block stop, which is how you say, no, you're not done. PostToolUse fires after the tool already ran, so it's too late to stop the call, though it can still feed text back to Claude. A few events ignore blocking, like notification, SessionStart, and FileChange, show your standard error, and carry on. A pretool use guardrail that redacts instead of blocking. The matcher picks the tool to watch, say, bash, and an optional if clause narrows it to a specific command. So returning deny stops a dangerous call. The lesser known move is return updated input to rewrite the call, which is how you strip a secret out of a command and still let it run. When Claude compacts a long conversation, it drops a lot of details, but a SessionStart hook with the compact matcher runs right after a print short summary of the files you've been working on. That summary goes back into context, so Claude picks up where it was instead of starting cold. Hooks turns a rule Claude usually follows into one that it always follows. Reach past auto formatting, guard tools with pretool use, gate the turn with stop, and preserve stay across compact. The setup pays back the first time it catches something on a run you weren't watching.

question.en:
Read the article, then answer the question below.

You wrote a PreToolUse hook to stop a dangerous command. It spots the command correctly, writes a clear reason to standard error, and exits with code 1. You test it, and Claude runs the command anyway. The hook fired, the reason was printed, and nothing was blocked.

What went wrong?
question.fr:
Lisez l'article, puis répondez à la question ci‑dessous.

Vous avez écrit un hook PreToolUse pour arrêter une commande dangereuse. Il détecte correctement la commande, écrit une raison claire sur la sortie d'erreur standard et se termine avec le code 1. Vous le testez, et Claude exécute quand même la commande. Le hook s'est déclenché, la raison a été affichée, et rien n'a été bloqué.

Qu'est-ce qui a mal tourné ?

text.en: Exit code 1 does not block. Exit 2 is the blocking code, and it feeds standard error back to Claude as context.
text.fr: Le code de sortie 1 ne bloque pas. Le code 2 est le code bloquant, et il renvoie la sortie d'erreur standard à Claude comme contexte.

text.en: A PreToolUse hook cannot stop a call. Only a stop hook can refuse something.
text.fr: Un hook PreToolUse ne peut pas arrêter un appel. Seul un stop hook peut refuser une action.

text.en: The reason has to go to standard out as plain text before Claude will act on it.
text.fr: La raison doit être envoyée sur la sortie standard (standard out) en texte brut avant que Claude n'agisse dessus.

text.en: Exit codes are ignored on PreToolUse, so the hook has to return JSON instead.
text.fr: Les codes de sortie sont ignorés dans PreToolUse, donc le hook doit renvoyer du JSON à la place.

explanation.en: Yes, and this is the one that catches almost everyone. Exit 1 feels like an error but it is non-blocking, so the call goes ahead. Exit 2 blocks and hands your message to Claude to act on.
explanation.fr: Oui, et c'est celui qui piège presque tout le monde. Le code de sortie 1 donne l'impression d'une erreur mais il n'est pas bloquant, donc l'appel se poursuit. Le code de sortie 2 bloque et transmet votre message à Claude pour qu'il agisse en conséquence.

hint.en:
Exit code 0 means success, and if standard out is JSON, Claude parses it.

Only one non-zero exit code blocks a call. Every other code is logged, and Claude carries on regardless.
hint.fr:
Le code de sortie 0 signifie succès, et si la sortie standard contient du JSON, Claude l'analyse.

Un seul code de sortie non nul bloque un appel. Tous les autres codes sont consignés, et Claude poursuit l'exécution quoi qu'il en soit.

# Strip the redundant Write() allow rule the image seeds into

p = '/home/repl/.claude/settings.json'

    perms['allow'] = [r for r in perms.get('allow', []) if not r.startswith('Write(')]
    json.dump(settings, open(p, 'w'), indent=2)
except Exception:
    pass
PY''')

question.en:
Read the article, then answer the question below.

You want a dependency audit that runs against the queries repository every fifteen minutes and commits any fix straight to your default branch. A routine looks like the obvious fit, since there is nothing to host and the prompt never changes.

What do the routine guardrails mean for this plan?
question.fr:
Lisez l'article, puis répondez à la question ci-dessous.

Vous voulez un audit des dépendances qui s'exécute sur le dépôt queries toutes les quinze minutes et qui commit toute correction directement sur votre branche par défaut. Une routine semble être le choix évident, puisqu'il n'y a rien à héberger et que l'invite ne change jamais.

Que signifient les garde-fous des routines pour ce plan ?

text.en: Any interval is available, so fifteen minutes is fine, and the branch a run pushes to is set per trigger.
text.fr: Tout intervalle est disponible, donc quinze minutes conviennent, et la branche vers laquelle une exécution pousse est définie par déclencheur.

text.en: A schedule runs at most hourly, and each run starts from a fresh clone of the default branch and can push only to claude/ prefixed branches unless you loosen it per repo.
text.fr: Un planning s'exécute au maximum toutes les heures, et chaque exécution démarre à partir d'un clone frais de la branche par défaut et ne peut pousser que vers des branches préfixées par claude/ à moins que vous ne l'assouplissiez par dépôt.

text.en: Runs push to the default branch by default, so you would need to add a restriction yourself.
text.fr: Par défaut, les exécutions poussent vers la branche par défaut, donc vous devriez ajouter vous-même une restriction.

text.en: Routines cannot touch a repository at all, so this job needs the GitHub action instead.
text.fr: Les routines ne peuvent pas du tout toucher un dépôt, donc ce travail nécessite plutôt l'action GitHub.

explanation.en: Right on the money. The plan needs two changes: an hourly schedule at the fastest, and a pull request from the claude/ branch instead of a commit to your default branch. That guardrail is what makes an unattended run safe to leave running.
explanation.fr: Exactement. Le plan nécessite deux changements : un planning horaire au maximum, et une pull request depuis la branche claude/ au lieu d'un commit direct sur votre branche par défaut. Ce garde-fou est ce qui rend une exécution non supervisée sûre à laisser tourner.

hint.en:
A routine bundles a prompt, a repository, and any connectors it needs, then runs on a cron schedule, an HTTP POST, or a GitHub event.

One of the guardrails exists specifically to stop an autonomous run from rewriting your default branch.
hint.fr:
Une routine regroupe un prompt, un dépôt et les connecteurs nécessaires, puis s’exécute selon un calendrier cron, une requête HTTP POST ou un événement GitHub.

L’un des garde-fous sert précisément à empêcher une exécution autonome de réécrire votre branche par défaut.

instructions.en: Classify each job as a fit for a routine, headless mode, or the Agent SDK.
instructions.fr: Classez chaque tâche selon qu’elle convient à une routine, au mode headless ou à l’Agent SDK.

text.en: A dependency audit every morning, with no machine of yours left on overnight.
text.fr: Un audit des dépendances chaque matin, sans qu'aucune de vos machines ne reste allumée pendant la nuit.

text.en: A triager that fires whenever a new pull request lands, using a prompt that never changes.
text.fr: Un triage qui se déclenche chaque fois qu'une nouvelle pull request arrive, en utilisant un prompt qui ne change jamais.

text.en: A build step that pipes a diff into Claude and reads the answer back as JSON for the next script.
text.fr: Une étape de build qui envoie un diff à Claude et lit la réponse sous forme de JSON pour le script suivant.

text.en: A job that needs a database and credentials which only exist on your build machine.
text.fr: Une tâche qui nécessite une base de données et des identifiants n'existant que sur votre machine de build.

text.en: A feature inside your own application that streams Claude's messages to your users.
text.fr: Une fonctionnalité intégrée à votre application qui diffuse en continu les messages de Claude à vos utilisateurs.

text.en: A TypeScript service that calls Claude with its own system prompt and allowed tools on every request.
text.fr: Un service TypeScript qui appelle Claude avec son propre system prompt et ses outils autorisés à chaque requête.

feedback.en: Well sorted. Start at the managed end and move down the spectrum only when the job demands it: a routine when nothing needs hosting, headless mode when the job needs your pipeline, and the Agent SDK when the work belongs inside your own product.
feedback.fr: Bien organisé. Commencez par l'extrémité gérée et descendez le spectre seulement quand le travail l'exige : une routine quand rien n'a besoin d'hébergement, le mode headless quand le travail nécessite votre pipeline, et l'Agent SDK quand le travail doit s'intégrer à votre propre produit.

hint.en:
Routines run on Anthropic's infrastructure with nothing for you to host, fired by a cron schedule, an HTTP POST, or a GitHub event.

Headless mode with -p is a one-shot command that reads standard in and writes standard out, so it pipes like any other shell tool.

The Agent SDK is a library that embeds Claude Code inside your own TypeScript or Python application.
hint.fr:
Les routines s'exécutent sur l'infrastructure d'Anthropic sans rien à héberger de votre côté, déclenchées par une planification cron, un HTTP POST ou un événement GitHub.

Le mode headless avec -p est une commande ponctuelle qui lit l'entrée standard et écrit la sortie standard, donc il se pipe comme n'importe quel autre outil de shell.

L'Agent SDK est une bibliothèque qui intègre Claude Code dans votre propre application TypeScript ou Python.

blocks.transcript:
1. Video: GitHub Actions and Code Review
The best place to hand off repetitive work is the pull request. There are two ways to get that. The managed one is code review, an anthropic hosted service that reviews PRs through the Claude GitHub app and posts findings as inline comments with nothing for you to build or host. The do-it-yourself one is the Claude Code GitHub action for when the job goes beyond review and into custom CI. An organization admin turns it on from the Claude Code admin settings, then installs the Claude GitHub app, and picks which repos it watches and when it runs. Once when a PR opens on every push, or only when someone comments at Claude, review. And from there, it runs on Anthropic's infrastructure. A set of review agents analyzes the diff against the full codebase and posts findings as inline comments on the specific lines, tagged by severity with a summary table and the check run. It deduplicates and ranks so you read a handful of real findings instead of a wall of nits. It never approves or blocks the PR, the judgment call stays with a human. Code review is a research preview, currently for team and enterprise plans, so expect the behavior to keep on moving. And there's no managed autofix, the service posts findings only. Applying them is a local move from your own terminal where the /code-review command reviews a diff and its --fix flag applies the findings to your working tree. The action covers the jobs beyond review, implementing changes from a comment, schedule reports, anything you'd write a workflow for. It runs the agent on PR comments, schedule jobs and any GitHub event. So from inside Claude Code, you can run the /install-github-app command. And you need repo admin to do this. The slash command walks you through installing the GitHub app and setting the Anthropic API key secret on the repo. The action itself is Anthropic's slash Claude Code action at V1. And the inputs you'll use is the Anthropic API key, which is required. The GitHub token, which defaults to secret.github token, the trigger phrase, which is what the action listens for in comments, which just defaults to at Claude. If you use bedrock or vertex, you can switch to those providers, the prompt, which is the instruction for the run, and then the Claude arguments, which is a string of CLI arguments passed through to Claude Code. So if you drop this into dot GitHub slash workflows slash Claude dot YAML, it listens for at Claude on PR comments and issue comments. So someone writes at Claude, implement the spec and the linked linear issue on a pull request. And the action picks it up. Claude pushes commits and post comments with what it did. This one's the daily roll up. Cron fires at nine UTC. The action runs Claude post the results. The workflow dispatch trigger also lets you run it manually from the actions tab. So the Claude args line is where all this fine tuning happens. I set the max turns to five. This just puts a hard cap on the agent loop permission mode. I put don't ask. This is the unattended mode. Allow tools is exactly what this job needs. So read only for a report for PR reviews. Take the managed path, enable code review, let the GitHub app post inline findings and apply fixes locally with /code-review --fix reach for the action when the job is more than review, install GitHub app for setup one workflow for at Claude mentions one for Cron all the tuning and Claude arcs.

question.en:
Read the article, then answer the question below.

Code Review is enabled on the queries repository. It reviews a pull request and posts three inline findings, one of them a real bug. Your teammate is now waiting for Claude to approve the pull request and push the fix. An hour later, nothing has happened.

What did they misunderstand, and how does the fix actually get applied?
question.fr:
Lisez l'article, puis répondez à la question ci‑dessous.

Code Review est activé sur le repository queries. Il examine une pull request et publie trois findings inline, dont l'un est un vrai bug. Votre coéquipier attend maintenant que Claude approuve la pull request et pousse le correctif. Une heure plus tard, rien ne s'est passé.

Qu'ont-ils mal compris, et comment le correctif est-il réellement appliqué ?

text.en: The findings need an @claude review comment before Claude will act on them.
text.fr: Les findings nécessitent un commentaire de review @claude avant que Claude n'agisse.

text.en: Code Review applies a fix automatically once a finding is tagged at a high enough severity.
text.fr: Code Review applique automatiquement une correction dès qu'une constatation est marquée avec une sévérité suffisamment élevée.

text.en: Approval is automatic once no findings remain, so the outstanding bug is what is holding it up.
text.fr: L'approbation est automatique dès qu'il ne reste plus de constatations, donc c'est le bug en suspens qui bloque le processus.

text.en: Code Review never approves or blocks a pull request and has no managed autofix. It posts findings, and you apply them locally with /code-review --fix.
text.fr: Code Review n'approuve ni ne bloque jamais une pull request et n'a pas d'autocorrection gérée. Il publie des constatations, que vous appliquez localement avec /code-review --fix.

explanation.en: Nicely reasoned. The service finds and ranks, you decide and apply. Pull the branch down, run /code-review with the --fix flag to apply findings to your working tree, and the human judgment stays where it belongs.
explanation.fr: Bien raisonné. Le service détecte et classe, vous décidez et appliquez. Récupérez la branche, lancez /code-review avec le flag --fix pour appliquer les constatations à votre working tree, et le jugement humain reste là où il doit être.

hint.en:
The service posts findings as inline comments and leaves the judgment call with a human.

Applying a finding is a local move, made from your own terminal rather than by the hosted service.

instructions.en:
Start Claude Code with claude.

Ask Claude to create .github/workflows/claude.yaml that runs anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 when someone comments on a pull request.

Have it pass the API key from repository secrets, listen for the @claude trigger phrase, and tune the run in claude_args with a five-turn cap and a permission mode that never stops to ask.

Type /exit to exit Claude Code.
instructions.fr:
Lancez Claude Code avec `claude`.

Demandez à Claude de créer `.github/workflows/claude.yaml`, qui exécute `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` lorsqu’une personne commente une pull request.

Demandez-lui de transmettre la clé API depuis les secrets du dépôt, d’écouter la phrase de déclenchement `@claude` et de régler `claude_args` avec une limite de cinq tours et un mode d’autorisation qui ne s’interrompt jamais pour demander.

Saisissez `/exit` pour quitter Claude Code.

blocks.starterCode:
repl = connect('bash')
# Strip the redundant Write() allow rule the image seeds into
# ~/.claude/settings.json. Newer Claude Code versions warn about it on every
# launch, since file permission checks only match Edit() rules and
# Edit(/home/repl/**) already covers every file-editing tool.
repl.run_command('''python3 - <<'PY'
import json
p = '/home/repl/.claude/settings.json'
try:
    settings = json.load(open(p))
    perms = settings.get('permissions', {})
    perms['allow'] = [r for r in perms.get('allow', []) if not r.startswith('Write(')]
    json.dump(settings, open(p, 'w'), indent=2)
except Exception:
    pass
PY''')
repl.run_command('rm -f /home/repl/queries/.claude/settings.local.json')
repl.run_command('rm -rf /home/repl/queries/.github')
repl.run_command('cd /home/repl/queries && rm -f ~/.claude/history.jsonl'
                 # Transcripts outlive history.jsonl, so a previous exercise's
                 # answers would otherwise be graded as this one's.
                 ' && rm -rf ~/.claude/projects/-home-repl-queries && clear')

hint.en:
The trigger_phrase input is what the action listens for in comments, and it defaults to @claude.

claude_args is a plain string of CLI arguments handed straight to Claude Code, so --max-turns 5 and the permission mode both go in there.

An unattended run has nobody to answer a prompt, so the mode you want allows only pre-approved tools and denies the rest.
hint.fr:
L’entrée `trigger_phrase` correspond à ce que l’action écoute dans les commentaires ; sa valeur par défaut est `@claude`.

`claude_args` est une simple chaîne d’arguments CLI transmise directement à Claude Code : `--max-turns 5` et le mode d’autorisation y figurent donc tous deux.

Une exécution sans supervision ne dispose de personne pour répondre à un prompt ; le mode recherché n’autorise donc que les outils préapprouvés et refuse les autres.

blocks.transcript:
1. Video: Trust It: Verifying Unsupervised Runs
You handed Claude a task and let it run without watching every step. Now it says it's done, but before you ship that, you need a way to check work that you didn't even supervise. A check is what makes hands-off Claude Code safe to rely on. Verify in proportion to the rope that you gave the run. A short session where you watched the messages scroll by needs a glance. An unattended run or a job that fired in continuous integration with nobody in the loop actually needs a real check, because no one saw it happen. And when a run does go unattended at work, keep it in auto mode rather than bypass permissions. The classifier still reviews each action for danger. It never judges whether the code is right, though, so the verification bar stays where it was. Set that bar from how unsupervised this run was. So start with the diff itself, rather than Claude's summary of it. Run /code-review to walk the changes and flag issues. Then put your eyes on git diff. The trap is a tidy summary that reads fine while the diff touched a file that you honestly didn't even expect it to. Read what changed and read the files that were in the plan first. The real gate on an unsupervised run is whether the test passed and whether Claude ran them or only claimed that it did. Don't leave that to trust. Wire it as a hook so Claude can't skip it. A stop hook that runs your tests and refuses to end the turn on a failure, or a PostToolUse hook that lints and type checks after every edit. A hook that exists with code 2 feeds the failure straight back to Claude, which reads it and fixes it without you asking. The check fires on every run, whether or not you remember to ask. The subagent code review you'd run before a PR works here, too. Point it at an unsupervised run. Open a fresh session or subagent and have it review the change cold, with no memory of how the code was built. It has no stake in the approach and catches what the original run talked itself past. Make the check as serious as the run was unsupervised. Read the diff, turn the test into a hook that gates the turn, verify headless runs by their JSON result and exit code, and get a cold second opinion on anything that matters. Do that and Claude did it while I wasn't looking. No longer takes faith.

question.en:
Read the article, then answer the question below.

An overnight run on the queries project has finished. Nobody watched it. The summary is three tidy lines: the pending-orders query was refactored, its callers were updated, and all checks pass. You have to decide whether to ship it.

What is the first move?
question.fr:
Lisez l'article, puis répondez à la question ci‑dessous.

Une exécution de nuit sur le projet queries est terminée. Personne ne l'a regardée. Le résumé tient en trois lignes bien propres : la requête pending-orders a été refactorisée, ses appelants ont été mis à jour, et toutes les vérifications passent. Vous devez décider s'il faut le déployer.

Quelle est la première démarche ?

text.en: Read the summary closely and spot-check the files it names.
text.fr: Lisez attentivement le résumé et vérifiez ponctuellement les fichiers qu'il nomme.

text.en: Ask Claude in the same session how confident it is in the change.
text.fr: Demandez à Claude, dans la même session, quel est son niveau de confiance dans le changement.

text.en: Run /code-review over the changes, then read git diff yourself, starting with anything that was not in the plan.
text.fr: Exécutez /code-review sur les changements, puis lisez le git diff vous‑même, en commençant par tout ce qui n'était pas dans le plan.

text.en: Trust it, since the run was in auto mode and the classifier reviewed every action.
text.fr: Faites‑lui confiance, puisque l'exécution était en mode automatique et que le classificateur a examiné chaque action.

explanation.en: Nailed it. The trap on an unsupervised run is a tidy summary sitting on top of a diff that touched something unexpected. Reading the diff is the only thing that surfaces it.

hint.en:
The blocking exit code is 2, and it hands standard error back to Claude as context to act on.

tsc exits 1 when it finds type errors, and exit 1 does not block, so the hook has to translate the failure. Something like npx tsc --noEmit || exit 2 covers it.

The wiring goes under hooks.Stop in .claude/settings.json, which needs no matcher because it is not watching a tool.

tsc se termine avec 1 lorsqu'il trouve des erreurs de typage, et exit 1 ne bloque pas, donc le hook doit traduire l'échec. Quelque chose comme npx tsc --noEmit || exit 2 couvre cela.

Le câblage se place sous hooks.Stop dans .claude/settings.json, qui n'a pas besoin de matcher car il n'observe aucun outil.

blocks.transcript:
1. Video: Plugins
A setup you trust is worth more when your whole team runs it. Plugins are how Claude Code packages a setup and moves it between people. And there are two sides to that, using the plugins other people publish and packaging your own once you've built something worth sharing. A plugin is one installable unit. Where it lives sets how you install it. Inside a session, /plugin install the organization name at the plugin name does the same thing. For a team, add a private marketplace once with the /plugin marketplace add your organization slash Claude plugins or whatever you want to call it. And every install after that results through it with centralized discovery, version tracking, and updates. Now a plugin runs code on your machine with your privileges and its hooks fire on every matching tool call. Install it for the skills and you also get its PreToolUse and stop hooks whether you read them or not. A community plugin can ship a stop hook that calls out to a network endpoint and nothing in your configuration will warn you. See every hook, agent, and MCP server that it adds. Install plugins and add marketplaces only from sources that you truly trust. The in-app submission form posts to the community marketplace after Anthropic's automated review. And the official marketplace is curated on its own track. Reviewed isn't the same as trusted though, so check what it does. A plugin doesn't overwrite your configuration. Its components run alongside yours. So first, hooks stack together. A plugin's PreToolUse and your own both fire on every tool call, which is the reason you read the details first. Skills, agents, and commands are namespaced under the plugin name so they never clash. A plugin can also ship a settings.json file but a narrow one. So Claude Code honors only the agent and subagent status line keys. Setting agent promotes one of the plugins subagents to the main thread with a system prompt, tool, restrictions, and model. And enabling that plugin changes how Claude Code behaves by default, which is one of the main reasons to look before you even turn it on. So once you've built a .claude directory, instead of your team copying and pasting between machines, package it instead. A plugin bundles all of it as one version installable unit. Skills, subagents, hooks, and MCP server configs, plus the longer tail of the language server protocol servers, background monitors, themes, and a settings.json slice. The manifest lives at .claude-plugin/plugin.json and holds the name, version, description, and author. It's optional but leave it out and Claude Code discovers components by directory convention. The directory structure does the rest. The same .claude shape that you already use with skills with one folder per skill, agents with one markdown file per subagent, hooks slash hooksjson and .mcpjson all at the plugin root. Name is the only required field and it namespaces your skills as the company name, skill name. Version it like any other dependency. When you use plugins, read before you install. When you build one, package your .claude the moment it works. One manifest, one install, and the setup you trust reaches your entire team.

question.en:
Read the article, then answer the question below.

A teammate found a community plugin with an excellent test-writing skill and installed it across the team. It came from the community marketplace, so it had been through automated review, and the skill is genuinely good. They read the skill's description and nothing else.

What did they take on besides the skill?
question.fr:
Lisez l'article, puis répondez à la question ci‑dessous.

Un coéquipier a trouvé un plugin communautaire dans la place de marché communautaire avec une excellente skill d'écriture de tests et l'a installé pour toute l'équipe. Il provenait de la place de marché communautaire, donc il avait été soumis à une revue automatisée, et la skill est vraiment bonne. Ils ont lu la description de la skill et rien d'autre.

Qu'ont-ils accepté en plus de la skill ?

text.en: Nothing beyond the skill, since a plugin's other components stay inert until you invoke them.
text.fr: Rien d'autre que la skill, puisque les autres composants d'un plugin restent inertes tant que vous ne les invoquez pas.

text.en: A silent downgrade, because the plugin's hooks replace the ones they had already configured.
text.fr: Une rétrogradation silencieuse, car les hooks du plugin remplacent ceux qu'ils avaient déjà configurés.

text.en: Overwritten skills, wherever a plugin skill shares a name with one of their own.
text.fr: Skills écrasées, chaque fois qu'une skill du plugin porte le même nom qu'une des leurs.

text.en: Its hooks. A plugin's PreToolUse and Stop hooks fire on every matching tool call with your privileges, and nothing in your configuration warns you.
text.fr: Ses hooks. Les hooks PreToolUse et Stop d'un plugin se déclenchent à chaque appel d'outil correspondant avec vos privilèges, et rien dans votre configuration ne vous avertit.

explanation.en: Precisely. A plugin runs code on your machine, and installing it for the skills means taking its hooks too. A stop hook that calls out to a network endpoint would look no different from the outside, which is why you check what a plugin adds before turning it on.
explanation.fr: Exactement. Un plugin exécute du code sur votre machine, et l'installer pour les skills signifie aussi prendre ses hooks. Un stop hook qui effectue un appel vers un point de terminaison réseau ne se distinguerait pas de l'extérieur, c'est pourquoi vous vérifiez ce qu'un plugin ajoute avant de l'activer.

hint.en:
A plugin's components run alongside your own configuration rather than replacing any of it.

Reviewed is not the same as trusted, and automated review catches some things rather than everything.

# Strip the redundant Write() allow rule the image seeds into
# ~/.claude/settings.json. Newer Claude Code versions warn about it on every
# launch, since file permission checks only match Edit() rules and
# Edit(/home/repl/**) already covers every file-editing tool.

import json

try:

    json.dump(settings, open(p, 'w'), indent=2)
except Exception:

PY''')
repl.run_command('rm -rf /home/repl/queries/queries-verify')
repl.run_command('mkdir -p /home/repl/queries/.claude/skills/verify-changes')
# Written with printf rather than a heredoc: the skill's YAML frontmatter
# delimiters would otherwise sit at the start of a line and split this exercise.
repl.run_command(
    "printf '%s\\n' '---' 'name: verify-changes'"
    " 'description: Run after edits to source files. Runs the type check, reads the diff, confirms no check was weakened, and reports pass or fail with evidence.'"
    " '---' '' '# Verify changes' ''"
    " '1. Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and capture the output.'"
    " '2. Read `git diff` for the changes made in this turn.'"
    " '3. Confirm no check was loosened or skipped to make the run pass.'"
    " '4. Report pass or fail, quoting the output you relied on.'"
    " > /home/repl/queries/.claude/skills/verify-changes/SKILL.md"
)

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "npx tsc --noEmit || exit 2"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
EOF''')
repl.run_command('cd /home/repl/queries && rm -f ~/.claude/history.jsonl'
